I think it’s important too that you all see us as a resource as well as being people connected to our communities. So, for example, if there are a cluster of buildings in any one of our districts, we should also be alerted so that we can help and work with those residents and offer resources that we might find available to them as well, because I think that there are many times in the four months that I’ve been in office now, I’ve already encountered four buildings within my district that are in very bad condition, falling in disrepair, and completely related to this topic. And a few feet away from my district office that we didn’t even know if things were happening and they are connected to HPD or DOB, maybe to like telling their neighbors, but I think that closing the loop and seeing us as a resource is important as

well. So hopefully that’s something that we can add on, especially when there’s like more than one or one property manager that has many developments in our district.
Thank you, Council Member. We’ll definitely keep you on speed dial instead.

You know where to find us. Well, with that I– oh, yeah, I wanted to make this PSA, right, to the millions of people watching at home, billions– no. But to the press, right, as you cover this hearing and you cover what we’re talking about here today, I think it is very important to underscore the importance for New Yorkers to call 311, right? Buildings and their tenants, tenants and landlords should always try to talk to each other first. They should try to resolve issues first, but there are those landlords who are, you know, for one reason or another not doing as they should, and when you call 311, when you make that complaint and HPD is able to go out there and agencies are able to go out there, you build the data sets that are quite literally triggering all of these

actions by our agencies, the CONH program and countless others. So, to the millions of you watching– maybe dozens– to the millions of you watching, just really underscoring that point. And to the members of the administration, thank you so much for your testimony. We’re going to be moving to the public.
Thank you.
We’re just taking a two minute recess, and we will start up with the public comment. [break]

Alright. Chair Encarnacion will be right back, but I’m going to open the hearing for public testimony. I remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit

transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today’s hearing, please fill out and appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today’s hearing topic of the tenant harassment against immigrant New Yorkers and the Certificate of No Harassment program, including the following legislation, Intro. 839. If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms. You may also email written testimony to testimony@council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing. Audio and video recordings will not be accepted. And I will now call the first panel: Ibrahim Ramoul from Make the Road, Divya Korada, Urban Justice, Sebastian Perez, Legal Aid, and Katie Anderson, NYLAG. And we’re going to add Peter Estes to this panel from ANHD. And whoever is ready can begin.

Good morning, Council Members. My name is Divya Korada and I’m a Staff

Attorney with Urban Justice Center’s Safety Net Project. The Safety Net Project combines direct legal services, community organizing and policy advocacy to build social and economic justice for indigent New Yorkers. As a staff attorney I work primarily on eviction defense in the Bronx through the Right to Counsel program. While I’m here today to talk about the concerning pattern of landlord harassment of tenants that I've personally seen, the tenants I work with, I want to highlight that the tenants who face this discrimination are hesitant to testify because of the risk further harassment. Our office has encountered a troubling pattern of landlords targeting tenants based on their immigration status which has even led tenants to self-evict in some cases. We’ve seen landlords who systematically use the threat of immigration enforcement to prevent their tenants from asserting their rights, for example through making calls to 311. We recommended that HPD can and must take action against these landlords by aggressively litigating 70 proceedings and comprehensive HPs to limit these landlords' engagement with vulnerable tenants. We found that in

the Bronxtenants may not have pathways to legalize their status which makes them especially vulnerable in this climate. The tenants that we work with had individual meetings with our managing director for immigration advice. And this is partially what has empowered them to step up and take action. However, many legal services providers do not have these kinds of resources, and the city must do more to fund the resources for immigration advice in these situations. We’ve also seen landlords successfully utilize calls to ICE about tenants. A tenant I worked with refused to show up to court because his landlord had been telling him that ICE would show up at the courthouse. Through the course of this case after his landlord had actually asked me personally personally about his immigration status. This tenants was detained by ICE and my office had to scramble to find immigration support for him. This is something we were able to do because we had the recourse, but ultimately, legal services providers do need to be able to provide this time of life as well.
Thank you.

Good morning. My name is Ibrahim Ramoul and I’m a housing attorney a Make the Road, a community-based organization representing tenants in Brooklyn and Queens. We represent 100s of tenants each year in eviction proceedings, legal lockouts, HP cases, and 7As. Make the Road fully supports the proposal to expand and make permanent HPD’s Certificate of No Harassment program. Indeed, in the past year we have seen a worrying uptick in landlord harassment and threats related to tenant’s perceived or actual immigration status. Particularly, we’re very concerned with the increasing number of tenants who have received threats by the landlords to call ICE or have had ICE been called on them. These threats are often leveled not just as retaliation, as Chair Sanchez mentioned in the introduction, but also in an attempt to secure an outcome for the landlord that they would otherwise not be entitled to. For example, we’ve had landlords threaten to call ICE if a tenant didn’t vacate within 10 days, and we know there’s no eviction process scheduled or no court proceeding in the works. We’ve also had a landlord threaten to

call ICE when a tenant did not pay a new higher rent that the landlord had decided they wanted to charge, even though they had not offered a corresponding lease agreement. There are obviously laws in place and institutions, corresponding institutions where these issues are dealt with. Sometimes however, they can feel inadequate as has been said often now for starters when a political climate when immigrant tenants are understandably very hesitant to seek out state or local agencies, law enforcement, or other resources that are meant to help them. We’ve had members at Make the Road, for example, who have shared with us that their landlord threatened to call ICE on them, but who are too afraid to even tell us the full story even anonymously for fear of retaliation. Some of the forums are also understaffed or underfunded and are not set up to provide suitable and timely remedy, at least not on their own. For example, the fines and compensation structure in Housing Court can sometimes not be enough or it may not deter landlords from continuing to engage in this unlawful behavior. So as a result in our– it’s the case in our practice usually that

harassment counter claims are worked in with other issues during settlement negotiations and it’s historically not a strong incentive to seek out harassment findings specifically [inaudible] landlords versus obtaining some rent reduction or related benefit which would benefit the tenant. So we, you know, support this pilot program and we think it’s be a great– another avenue for tenants to pursue justice. Thank you.
Thank you.

Good morning and thank you for the opportunity to testify in support of this legislation. My name’s Katie Anderson. I’m a staff attorney at New York Legal Assistance Group in the Tenants’ Rights Unit. Across all of NYLAG’s programs we represent immigrant communities including in True [sic] where we represent immigrants and their families as they’re being evicted. And in our practice at True we’ve seen alarming pattern of landlords attempting to circumvent the legal proceeding for an eviction, for starting a new eviction case by threatening retaliation against our clients based on their immigration status. This

pattern is across many different housing types from rent stabilized apartments to public housing, to even superintendent apartments. One of our clients in a rent stabilized apartment had his landlord stop accepting rent and told him if he did not vacate his apartment, that he would call ICE, even though no formal eviction process had been commenced at that point. Another immigrant client in public housing was told by a NYCHA employee they would call ICE if he continued to try to assert his son’s [sic] rights to the apartment. And in another case, an undocumented client of ours was working as a super where his only compensation was his apartment. When he found an employment complaint, his landlord started multiple eviction proceedings against him to the point that our client left the apartment and self-deported back to the D.R. The threat of retaliation deeply impacts our clients as there’s little recourse available for this behavior, especially since many of our clients don’t want to go on the record in Housing Court on these issues and face further retaliation. Housing is just one of the ways our immigrant clients face this harassment in

their day-to-day lives, and this proposed legislation is a meaningful step towards extending protection and accountability, with our immigrant clients being especially vulnerable to harassment and retaliation. Based on their immigration status, it’s our sincere hope that City Council will make this pilot program permanent and ensure that immigrant New Yorkers are not harassed out of their homes.

Good morning, Chair Sanchez, and Chair Encarnacion. My name is Sebastian Perez and I am staff attorney with the Legal Aid Society– that was fast– the Legal Aid Society’s Housing Justice Group Advocacy Unit in Manhattan. Thank you for the opportunity to testify in support of the proposed enhancement to the Certificate of No Harassment program. While this program is a vital shield against unlawful displacement, our practice sees firsthand how the current framework can leave our city’s most vulnerable neighborhood, particularly immigrant tenants exposed to predatory tactics. As the Council is aware, harassment is defined by any act or omission intended to force a awful occupant to surrender their rights to vacate their home. For

immigrant New Yorkers, this harassment often takes a specific sinister form. The threat of ICE or DHS involvement and deportation. His glooming threat creates a silence tax where tenants endure illegal living conditions out of the fear of retaliation. Our case stories illustrate why we need more robust protections and earlier triggers proposed in our recommendations. For example, in Manhattan we represent tenants who live without heat or hot weather for a full decade. They remain silent because their landlord told them that as immigrants they had no rights and that any complaint would result in ICE removal. It was only when the building lost all water and electricity this year that they felt they had no choice but to seek legal help. In the Bronx, a landlord attempted to dismantle a tenant association by threatening to call ICE residents for simply meeting in the lobby. The landlord went as far a posting physical notice throughout the building using federal immigration enforcement as a tool to suppress organized advocacy. A second case in the Bronx, after an immigrant family with minor children refused an illegal $700 rent increase on the

mis-classified market rate unit. The landlord filed a false criminal complaint with ICE and left copies of the filing on the families’ doorstep to terrorize them. We are currently seeking a permanent injunction to stop this egregious behavior. These are not isolated incidents, they are every day reality for immigrant tenants, because an ultimate legal finding of harassment is notoriously difficult to secure and often requires years of litigation. We urge the Council to incorporate earlier triggers for CONH required lists. We cannot wait for the most egregious cases to reach a final judgement. Before the program's connections kick in, by then the damage is often done and tenants are often gone.
You conclude? SEBASTIAN PEREZ Yes.
Yes, okay. Alright, thank you.

Good morning and thank you to the Committee Chairs Sanchez and Encarnacion and members of the committees for the opportunity to testify today. My name is Peter Estes and I’m senior housing policy associate at the Association for

Neighborhood and Housing Development. ANHD is composed of over 80 community-based organizations working toward housing, economic and racial justice all across the city. Tenant harassment is one of the most pernicious tools of displacement. Landlords neglect essential services, ignore repairs, use unpermitted construction to make homes unlivable, and inundate tenants with unsolicited buyout offers. These tactics are wielded most effectively against those with fewest resources to fight back, elderly and disabled tenants, mixed-status families and low income New Yorkers. As highlighted clearly today, our immigrant neighbors face additional layers of harassment. ANHD members reported landlords– an increase in landlords calling ICE on tenants who organized to improve building conditions, targeting them through discriminatory racial and ethnic profiling. These chilling acts come against the backdrop of intensified federal attacks on immigrants and require urgent action. We must do everything in our power at the local level to reaffirm our commitment to safety through community and strong, stable neighborhoods. The CONH program is a critical

tool to deter harassing behavior. ANHD helped lead the original campaign for the program passed in 2018 and improved by the Council in 2021 which targets buildings at elevated risk of harassment. When an owner of a listed building seeks permits for covered categories of alterations, they must first demonstrate that no harassment has occurred or face a five-year freeze on permits that put tenants at risk of displacement with an option to cure the denial by providing permanently affordable housing. The program covers just 2.5 percent of eligible buildings, perhaps too few, but it is working to identify the buildings where tenants are most at risk. Denial rates are significantly higher than incomparable CONH programs, and buildings on the list have seen noteworthy reductions in violations relative to similar buildings. I have a few–
[interposing] You may conclude.

ANHD strongly supports making the program permanent with a few targeted improvements. First, extending protections portfolio-wide when a landlord is denied a CONH.

Similar spirit as the proposed changes from the Council Member’s current bill, but maybe go beyond. Two, requiring a CONH before any building sale to interrupt cycles of displacement. Recalculating the building qualification index annually rather than every five years, and retaining buildings with pre-2021 harassment findings so that landlords cannot simply age out of accountability for actions during some of the most tumultuous years in our city. We also do not think that HPD’s proposed changes to the cure presented in their report which would replace the affordable housing requirement with an independent monitor is sufficient deterrent for a meaningful consequence. I have other recommendations related to strengthening the program that we’ve discussed and their included in my written testimony. Thank you again for the opportunity to testify.
Thank you.
I just want to say thank you. I know many of you have actually worked with some of the residents in my district specifically in some of the cases, and so I just thank you for the work that you do.

Thank you, Chair. I just have one follow-up question on the many stories that you all highlighted. So, are you in every instance pursuing a finding of harassment in these cases, and if you are, you know, what are the time drivers or what are the barriers to that finding being ruled by the judge?

I can start. One of the biggest barriers is obviously in a Housing Court the record is public so many of our clients don’t want to have that be on the public record, and we are always cognizant of that and sometimes we’re talking circles around these. Also, it can be very difficult to find a harassment finding in Housing Court. You would have to go to trial. That obviously exposes clients to a lot of risk in that sense, too, and you know, depending on the kind of case at the end of the day, even if a judge finds harassment, they might just say, well, you still owe $50,000 in rent. So, it’s– there’s a lot of complicating factors to actually pursuing that in Housing Court.
Judges don’t award damages or anything like that when there’s–

[interposing] They could, but it would also– but they can still say that there’s still rent that’s owed and ultimately in a lot of nonpayment cases, that’s what judges are focused on, at least in my experience.
Okay. And are you always filing for harassment?
At least in my case, it depends on the client how much they want to be included on the record.

So, the stories that you’re sharing with us– I mean, it would– we would love to follow up, would love to just understand the breakdown of how often you did file, whether CONH should, you know, consider anything different in our own– and the determination that we’re enabling HPD to find.

To answer I think one of your later questions, we– well, I, at least, we always try to include harassment in our pleadings, because it’s such a broad definition that it’s kind of easy to meet when our clients are telling us the stories of why they want to pursue litigation to

begin with. And then the difficult part, I think just to kind of piggyback off of that is yes, it requires– the presumption is that a finding of harassment, you have done all this leg work up front, that you have found a client– if you’ve been working a group, you’ve been able to form a group together that kind of wants to move forward to begin with, and then you get the initial court date then the second court date. If you need a hearing, and once again, that’s all presumed to have happened if you are requiring a final determination of harassment.

Thank you. Thank you so much, and we’ll– we’d love to follow up with you. Thank you. The next panel will consist of Anna Baker-Heans, Cooper Square Committee, Van Xelo from Mixteca, Thomas Duklett, Ruihra– apologies if I’m mispronouncing that– Ruihra Lubega, and Zachary Hall. And whoever is ready can begin.

Hi, can you hear me? Okay. Good morning– or good afternoon. My name is Anna Baker-Heans. I’m a tenant organizer with Cooper Square Committee, and I’m speaking on behalf of a tenant I organize with, and I just want to note that

three of us here are all testifying about the same building. So, now I’m switching to my tenant’s testimony: “Good afternoon. My name is Shera Beckwith [sp?]. I have been a tenant at 109 East 9th Street which is a single-room occupancy building since 1992. When we got a new landlord a few years ago, I learned about the CONH program from the HPD investigator who is responsible for determining if the landlord should get a CONH or not. The landlord was successful in getting a CONH, and as soon as he got it, he moved to evict me and some other tenants, and significantly stepped up his harassment in other ways. My buildings tenants association was successful in having his CONH rescinded this year with a ton of help from Take Root Justice and Cooper Square Committee. Without this help, I would have already lost my home and I think other tenants would be way worse off. Even though we had a bumpy road with the CONH program, I believe the CONH program is good and necessary. Since the CONH has been rescinded, the landlord hasn’t been able to do any further major work on the building where he had proposed construction, including removing the roof

and having all of the tenants move out for an unspecified period of time. I am definitely in favor of landlords needing Certificates of No Harassment. In my experience, the current program is far from perfect and needs some work. My landlord should not have been able to get one in the first place and it required a full trial at OATH, the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings, to get it rescinded. But at the same time, I can imagine that without this program tenants in situations like ours would be way worse off. I hope you will vote to make this CONH program permanent and will work with tenants who have gone through the program to improve it and better protect us. And some of my fellow neighbors who are here today will provide some specific suggestions for how they believe the CONH program can be improved.” And when we circle back to questions, I, Anna, a tenant organizer would love to speak more to the question that you, Council Member Sanchez, asked about the ability to get repairs under the CONH program. Thank you.
Thank you.

Good morning, Council Members. My name is Van. I’m the committee organizer at Mixteca, a community-based organization in Sunset Park, Brooklyn that serves immigrant, Latin, and indigenous communities for over 25 years. As a community-based organization that provides direct services to our community members, we’ve heard several stories of their lived experiences, many of which are around housing. We’ve heard stories of community members being harassed by their landlords or they’re being threatened to move out of their apartments or have ICE called on them. We’ve heard community members during Know Your Rights workshops share how they’re worried to ask for housing repairs because they’re unsure of how their status might impact the relationship with their landlords. Through our Know Your Rights workshops we try our best to inform our community members about their tenant rights regardless of their immigration status. But this is just one part of addressing these issues. This is why we should have the Intro 0839 be passed. Having the Certificate of No Harassment, the pilot program, become permanent would be creating an

additional solution around these harassments. Requiring property owners to undergo an investigation of harassment or of any violation of tenant’s rights would not only hold them accountable, but ensure there’s an end to these ongoing threats and coercion. There are many of our community members who are also not fully aware that you can look up building’s harassment history. On top of that, several of our community members also lack computer literacy in order to do this type of research. Having clear visible signage of any harassment filing against building owners for tenants to see would aid community members drastically. Being aware of the tenant– of the building owner’s harassment history and of their tenant rights would empower our community members to speak up when there is a housing repair that is needed to occur. Thank you so much for your time and hearing us all today.
Thank you. Zachary

Good morning. My name is Zachary Hall. I am a tenant in an SRO building that until recently had a CONH. CONH programs help protect tenants from predatory landlords by ensuring

they cannot obtain permits or drastically alter their buildings if they’re engaging in harassing conduct. I believe that CONH programs are an important tool not just for SRO buildings but also other forms of affordable housing. I feel the CONH program should be expanded and redesigned to further protect tenants that have affordable housing. This program protected me and other tenants in my building from having our homes taken from us by the landlord. To my mind, the person that bought our building five years ago had a predatory intention. Because I am an SRO tenant, I ran a private room, but share a common area of facilities with my neighbors in the building, like showers, toilets, and kitchen. When our landlord purchased our building, he removed two of shared toilets, one of our showers, and the building's only kitchen. He told us he did this to cure an old DOB violation that he needed to secure a CONH to restore the shared facilities. At the time he applied for the CONH, I wasn’t aware that this conduct counted as harassment. I was under the impression that was in the more common sense of the world. After he secured the CONH, the landlord started doing construction on

vacant units in the building but did not restore shared facilities, and he started to try to convince my neighbors and I to move out. We became concerned that the landlord might be trying to displace us. After months of organizing with my neighbors and diligent communication with HPD about the issues we were facing, HPD found probable cause for harassment and initiated a case in the office of Administrative Trials and Hearings to rescind the building’s CONH. during the trial, the OATH judge concluded that the landlord provided on credible evidence that he removed our essential services to clear a DOB violation, even when the landlord was supposed to prove it in court. The judge concluded that tenant harassment had occurred by the landlord, and the building CONH was rescinded, which means that our landlord can longer pursue redeveloping our building for at least three years after which he will be eligible to apply for a CONH unit I have a little bit more.
You may conclude.

ONe way I think the CONH program can be improved is by helping ensure NYDC

tenants are better informed of the various forms of tenant harassment that can occur. There are a vast array of tactics and loopholes that new landlords could use to pressure long-standing tenants with affordable rents. In fact, I've seen multiple websites that reference the CONH as just a mere formality to acquire in the pursuit to redevelop the building. Had we been better informed by the city and the CONH program about all the possible forms of harassment, we may have been able to prevent the landlord from receiving a CONH in the first place. However, the CONH program still protected us in the long-run by creating important checks and balances that help protect tenants. I hope that you will vote to make the CONH program permanent, and if anything, figure out methods to expand it. I hope you can also find ways for tenants to be made better aware of their rights and help them identify and understand the true meaning of what constitutes tenant harassment. Thank you.
Thank you.

[inaudible] read the three minutes into two. I’ve just got a list of

things. [inaudible] addressed. Thomas Duklett, the resident 109 East 9th street, Manhattan. We’ve endured harassment followed by the landlord CONH application over which I learned of course doesn't [inaudible] the application. And ongoing problems since the OCNH’s and extraordinary recision following a court finding of harassment at the OATH court. An entry signage rule should be considered to direct tenants to information about how to recognize and report harassment and protections for doing so. Complaints, you need to be allowed some form of free text for when drop-down forms are inadequate to describe the problem. HPD complaint forms are especially problematic in not allowing many complaints to be filed, merely because the drop-down field does not provide a means to properly identify the location or nature of the problem. Inspectors should be able to gain access and due course of time and not merely close complaints for landlord refusal to provide access. Effective protection of tenants should not have some complaint or violation inspectors presumptively giving landlords the benefit of the doubt. Tenants almost always exhausted the

cooperative approach when they have finally made complaints. Some inspectors presuming that it’s generally overstate complaints and that landlords should not be bothered by complaints relating to fundamental building functions simply ignore the world world. Yes, I’ve met such inspectors. Landlords should not have blanket allowance to self-certify curing violations, especially when they have a problematic pattern of complaints or suspicion of harassment. Tenants should have some means of providing information to violation hearings. Landlords all too easily act with impunity for having violations repeatedly dismissed for benign given the benefit of the doubt when falsely claiming the violations have been cured or never actually just in the first place. Outstanding violations should have enforcement. There should be no presumption that landlords are above enforcement.
You may conclude.

The CONH application process should be accompanied by notices posted in common areas and in individually distributed to tenants guiding tenants to resources describing the

function, the risk of landlords having a CONH and how to effectively allow to oppose CONH which would be recognized by the CONH issuing agency. Risks identified should include how to discover real world information about what landlords can do and have done to undermine tenant protections after being granted a CONH. CONH application investigators inquiring of tenants should have training about recognizing tenant intimidation and coercion and acting for such a process.
And you can submit all of this testimony, if you want to wrap up.

Tenants in the building where I’ve experienced accelerated efforts to drive us out,- after the CONH was suspended and even rescinded– I’d like to raise a point that I think Anna said she’d go back to in some questions. When the landlords is [inaudible] destroyed the housing units and essential facilities without a CONH, there should be some process for restoring those facilities without granting a CONH. Granting a CONH for harassing destruction would be rewarding the landlords for that destruction. There is no obvious

resolution to get to an impasse between some types of repairs and a lack of a CONH, but Council should be cautioned against opening a loophole for abuse. A possible resolution might involve a very limited exemption with a carefully constrained contract to which all parties agree, but the law may not allow for such contracts. Changing the law to provide an exemption could too easily make any CONH protections meaningless. So, please be careful.

Thank you. Thank you so much for those additional ideas. Please do submit them so that we can– we have them during the amendment consideration process. I did want to follow up on your earlier point about the tenant perspective on whether a CONH holds back any necessary work?

Thank you so much. And I want to start with just like a quick disclaimer that the three of us are speaking about an SRO building, so that’s part of a CONH program prior to this pilot program, and I’m not sure if there’s like nuance in how repairs can or cannot be made. That’s different between like the SRO buildings and the

pilot program buildings. But the tenants have spoken to the fact that their landlord removed their common area facilities, so all tenants only have access to two toilets, one shower, and no kitchen in their building. And he also– the landlord also gutted vacant apartments which can be a fire hazard. DOB has asserted that the building is completely safe for tenants to be in, and we completely agree, but since the CONH has been rescinded, DOB and HPD have asserted that a CONH would be required to restore common facilities and to restore the gutted apartments. We don’t agree with that stance. We think that there should be room for very specific, as Thomas said, and supervised work to add to tenant safety and their experience at the building, but we have to be really careful about, like, what kind of work is allowed so that landlords aren’t taking advantage of this to make conditions worse for tenants, but in the experience of the tenants at 109, they have not been able to get repairs or services restored in ways that they’d like.
Got it. Thank you. That’s very helpful, and it sounds like more of an exception to the general rule than–
[interposing] We’re not exactly sure the difference. I think it’d be worth following up with
Okay, great.
[inaudible]
Sir, we do have to move forward, but last comment and then we’ll go.
[inaudible] follow [inaudible]

I also feel that the consequences for landlord committing tenant harassment are very low and perhaps this program can deal with these matters. In our case, once the landlord acquired a CONH, the harassment against tenants increased exponentially as if he proved he didn’t harass tenants. He continues his harassments with us with little to actually deter even after the CONH has been revoked.

Got it. Okay. Thank you. Thank you so much for testifying today,

and I look forward to your testimony in writing. There was one person we’d called before. Just making sure she’s not here or they’re not here. Ruihra Lubega? So Lubega will be first, and then we have Amadou Ly, Amar Dieng, Gora Ndiaye, Mdeye Sire Mdiuka, Chiekh Diaw, and Moustpha Kane. I think they might be– they might be next door, so come on over and testify. Good to see you. Let me read them again. Amar Dieng, Gora Ndiaye, Mdeye Sire Mdiuka, Chiekh Diaw, and Moustpha Kane. Okay, I think the best place is for you to sit next to the microphone and the person who you are translating to, they switch. Is that okay? But Mr. Lubega, do you want to go first? You speak English, yeah?
Yes.
Perfect. So, Mr. Lubega can start and then we go with those who need the translation support.

Good afternoon. [inaudible] I’m a transgender man. I’m a migrant from Uganda. I’m here to complain about [inaudible] that shelter located in Queens. It is under designation [sic] tomorrow. Last year, I was bitten, and I was–

they took me to the hospital. I’ve tried to reach out to DHS to civil human right defenders to see that they advocate for me. I never got support. As I migrant, I’m in this country I love. I ran out of my country back home, Uganda, to seek for safety as a transgender person. But that way they treat me at the shelter is not good. Sometimes I feel even like ending my life. I work as a home health aide. I work 36 hours. I told them that please help me at least you get me for a settle [sic] voucher [sic]. I know I’m hardworking. I– after the lease, I will manage to pay for that rent. I give them all my information, but when the package came back, they just told me that there’s some information that was not there. When I tried to reach out to the program’s director, the shelter, Mr. Sherry [sp?], is the same woman that told that case worker to fight me. I have their pictures. By the time when I was in the hospital, she just told me that I should go back to my home country. This is not my country. So, I wasn’t supposed to be treated like that. Back home I have not my family. They disowned me. I come here. I’m learning this country. Why is that I’m being

treated like that? I don’t [inaudible] for the shelter. They don’t give me anything.
